items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The Qing reform programme of c. 1861–1895 that adopted Western military technology and industry while preserving Confucian institutions"?
items.answer: Self-Strengthening Movement
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of Self-Strengthening Movement.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Self-Strengthening Movement and the late Qing New Policies (1901–1911).
items.answer: Self-Strengthening adopted Western technology while preserving traditional institutions; the New Policies went further, abolishing the examination system (1905), creating a New Army and planning a constitution, but they came too late and empowered opponents.
items.markingKey: Self-Strengthening adopted Western technology while preserving traditional institutions; the New Policies went further, abolishing the examination system (1905), creating a New Army and planning a constitution, but they came too late and empowered opponents. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that the 1911 Revolution transformed Chinese society. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It ended imperial rule but left social structures, landlord power and poverty largely intact; real power passed to military leaders.
items.markingKey: It ended imperial rule but left social structures, landlord power and poverty largely intact; real power passed to military leaders. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Sun Yat-sen led the Wuchang Uprising in October 1911." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Sun was in the USA when the uprising began; it was started by New Army soldiers influenced by revolutionary groups, and Sun returned to become provisional president in January 1912.
items.markingKey: Sun was in the USA when the uprising began; it was started by New Army soldiers influenced by revolutionary groups, and Sun returned to become provisional president in January 1912. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the Qing dynasty collapsed because of foreign imperialism rather than internal weakness? [15]
items.answer: Foreign imperialism exposed and deepened internal weaknesses, but internal failures determined the timing and form of collapse.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: defeats in the Opium Wars and the 1894–95 war with Japan; Boxer indemnity bankrupted the state; foreign loans and railway concessions; corruption and weak central authority; Han nationalism against the Manchus; reforms that empowered the gentry and the New Army. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Foreign imperialism exposed and deepened internal weaknesses, but internal failures determined the timing and form of collapse. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Self-Strengthening Movement"?
options: The Qing reform programme of c. 1861–1895 that adopted Western military technology and industry while preserving Confucian institutions
Sun Yat-sen’s political programme of nationalism (minzu), democracy (minquan) and the people’s livelihood (minsheng)
“Japan and Korea as one body”: the assimilation policy of the late 1930s that forced Koreans to adopt Japanese names and worship at Shinto shrines
The army mutiny in Wuchang on 10 October 1911 that sparked the revolution against the Qing dynasty
items.answer: The Qing reform programme of c. 1861–1895 that adopted Western military technology and industry while preserving Confucian institutions
items.markingKey: A. "Self-Strengthening Movement" is the Qing reform programme of c. 1861–1895 that adopted Western military technology and industry while preserving Confucian institutions.

items.stem:
Source B
The revolution of 1911 was less the work of the revolutionaries than of the dynasty’s own reforms. The New Army, the provincial assemblies and the gentry who demanded railway rights all turned against a court that had raised expectations it could not meet.
— Jonathan Spence, historian, The Search for Modern China (1990) (paraphrased)

What is the message conveyed by Source B? [2]
items.answer: The 1911 Revolution resulted mainly from the Qing’s own reforms; the New Army, assemblies and gentry turned against the court; rising expectations were not met.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The GMD–CCP military campaign of 1926–1928 led by Chiang Kai-shek to defeat the warlords and unify China"?
items.answer: Northern Expedition
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Northern Expedition.

items.stem: "The Northern Expedition created a fully unified China under Chiang Kai-shek." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Unification was nominal: many warlords kept their armies and regional power by joining the GMD, and the CCP had been purged and continued in rural bases.
items.markingKey: Unification was nominal: many warlords kept their armies and regional power by joining the GMD, and the CCP had been purged and continued in rural bases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the New Culture Movement and the May Fourth protests.
items.answer: The New Culture Movement (from c. 1915) was an intellectual campaign against Confucianism led by Chen Duxiu’s journal New Youth; the May Fourth protests of 1919 were political demonstrations against the Versailles decision, which broadened the movement and linked it to nationalism.
items.markingKey: The New Culture Movement (from c. 1915) was an intellectual campaign against Confucianism led by Chen Duxiu’s journal New Youth; the May Fourth protests of 1919 were political demonstrations against the Versailles decision, which broadened the movement and linked it to nationalism. items.stem:
Source C
We must save the nation. Our country is being swallowed by Japan, and our own government has betrayed us at Paris. China’s territory may be conquered, but it cannot be given away; the Chinese people may be massacred, but they will not bow their heads.
— Manifesto of the students of Beijing, distributed on 4 May 1919 (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source C, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the warlord era, the May Fourth Movement and the Northern Expedition. [3]
items.answer: Value: It is a contemporary document from the protesters themselves, showing their nationalist motivation. Limitations: It is a mobilising manifesto, emotive in tone; it reflects students’ views rather than those of the wider population.
items.markingKey: Value: It is a contemporary document from the protesters themselves, showing their nationalist motivation. items.answer: China was being torn apart by rival warlords; foreign powers profited from the divisions; the nation was helpless.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the warlord era was a period of total disorder in China.
items.answer: Political fragmentation was severe, but the era also saw important cultural, intellectual and economic change.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: constant civil wars and banditry; no effective central government; heavy taxation of peasants. Arguments against: some warlords modernised regions (Yan Xishan in Shanxi); cultural and intellectual flourishing (May Fourth); growth of industry in treaty ports. Supported judgement: Political fragmentation was severe, but the era also saw important cultural, intellectual and economic change.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the May Fourth Movement was significant for Chinese politics.
items.answer: It fused nationalism with demands for modernisation (“Mr Science and Mr Democracy”), discredited Confucian tradition and Western liberal promises, and led many intellectuals such as Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao towards Marxism and the founding of the CCP in 1921.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It fused nationalism with demands for modernisation (“Mr Science and Mr Democracy”), discredited Confucian tradition and Western liberal promises, and led many intellectuals such as Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao towards Marxism and the founding of the CCP in 1921. items.stem: A student claims that the May Fourth Movement was only a student protest. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It began with students but spread to merchants and workers, with strikes and boycotts of Japanese goods in Shanghai and other cities.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Xi’an Incident"?

The alliance of the GMD and CCP from 1923 to 1927, brokered by the Comintern
The protests that began in Beijing on 4 May 1919 against the Versailles decision to transfer Germany’s rights in Shandong to Japan, which grew into a wider cultural and political movement
The GMD–CCP military campaign of 1926–1928 led by Chiang Kai-shek to defeat the warlords and unify China
items.answer: The kidnapping of Chiang Kai-shek in December 1936 by Zhang Xueliang, forcing him to agree to a Second United Front against Japan
items.markingKey: A. "Xi’an Incident" is the kidnapping of Chiang Kai-shek in December 1936 by Zhang Xueliang, forcing him to agree to a Second United Front against Japan.

items.stem: Explain why the Yan’an period was important for the CCP.

items.stem: Examine the view that the Qing dynasty collapsed because of foreign imperialism rather than internal weakness. Refer to at least two examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Foreign imperialism exposed and deepened internal weaknesses, but internal failures determined the timing and form of collapse.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. items.stem: Nia writes: "The Northern Expedition created a fully unified China under Chiang Kai-shek." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Unification was nominal: many warlords kept their armies and regional power by joining the GMD, and the CCP had been purged and continued in rural bases.

items.stem: "Japanese rule brought no economic development to Korea." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Japan built railways, ports and industry, especially in the north in the 1930s, but development served Japanese interests; rice was exported to Japan while Korean consumption fell.

items.stem: Distinguish between the GMD’s base of support and the CCP’s base of support.
items.answer: The GMD relied on urban elites, merchants, landlords and the army; the CCP built support among peasants through land policies, disciplined troops and anti-Japanese nationalism.

items.stem: Distinguish between the May Fourth protests and the New Culture Movement.
items.answer: The New Culture Movement (from c. 1915) was an intellectual campaign against Confucianism led by Chen Duxiu’s journal New Youth; the May Fourth protests of 1919 were political demonstrations against the Versailles decision, which broadened the movement and linked it to nationalism.
